patient.chief_complaint: Subacute right arm weakness and headaches, initially attributed to a TIA
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Marcus Webb is a 60-year-old right-handed Black man with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia who presents to the neurology inpatient service after transfer from an outside urgent care, where he was initially evaluated for suspected transient ischemic attack. His wife reports that approximately five weeks ago he began complaining of a dull, persistent headache predominantly over the left parietal region, worse upon waking in the morning and accompanied by occasional mild nausea. He and his wife initially attributed this to stress and tension headaches related to the end-of-school-year administrative work. Over the past three weeks, his wife noticed that he was using his right hand less fluidly: he dropped a coffee cup, had difficulty buttoning his shirt, and struggled with his usual handwriting. When she expressed concern, he attributed the clumsiness to 'sleeping on his arm wrong.' Approximately ten days ago, a colleague noticed he seemed to have difficulty seeing things on his right side; he walked into a door frame on the right twice in one week. His primary care physician was contacted by phone and, in the context of his cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, prior smoking, age), provisionally attributed the right-sided symptoms to a possible transient ischemic attack and planned outpatient neuroimaging. He was given aspirin, counseled on stroke precautions, and told to follow up in one week. Two days later, the symptoms had not resolved and his wife brought him to an urgent care facility, where an expedited non-contrast head CT was performed showing a large hyperdense lesion in the left posterior parietal region with surrounding hypodensity and approximately 7 mm of rightward midline shift. He was transferred to the neurology service for further evaluation. He denies fever, chills, weight loss, known malignancy, recent head trauma, or prior neurological disease. He has no history of seizures.

results.title: The 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System: a summary
results.authors: Louis DN, Perry A, Wesseling P, et al.
results.key_finding: The 2021 WHO CNS5 classification integrates histological and molecular criteria; glioblastoma is now defined as an IDH-wildtype astrocytic glioma with one or more of microvascular proliferation, necrosis, TERT promoter mutation, EGFR gene amplification, or +7/-10 chromosome copy-number changes, and is designated WHO grade 4 by definition.

results.title: Radiotherapy plus concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide for glioblastoma
results.authors: Stupp R, Mason WP, van den Bent MJ, et al.
results.key_finding: Concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide with radiotherapy improved median overall survival to 14.6 months versus 12.1 months with radiotherapy alone, establishing the standard-of-care chemoradiotherapy regimen for newly diagnosed glioblastoma.

results.title: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Central Nervous System Cancers
results.key_finding: Standard of care for newly diagnosed glioblastoma includes maximal safe resection, followed by concurrent chemoradiotherapy (60 Gy over 30 fractions with temozolomide 75 mg/m² daily), then adjuvant temozolomide and tumor-treating fields. Molecular profiling (IDH, MGMT, 1p/19q, TERT) is required for definitive WHO 2021 classification and informs prognosis.

general.summary: No directly applicable high-quality evidence retrieved for this query. Recommend correlating with current society guidelines.

differential.key_features: Ring-enhancing necrotic mass is compatible with metastasis; no known primary malignancy and infiltrative margins with deep white matter and corpus callosum splenium involvement favour primary glioma over metastasis

In immunocompetent patients, PCNSL typically presents as homogeneously enhancing, periventricular, diffusely DWI-restricting mass without central necrosis; necrotic ring enhancement argues strongly against
No fever, no leukocytosis, no systemic infectious source; ring enhancement is thick and irregular (not thin and smooth); central DWI restriction absent; rCBV markedly elevated rather than reduced

Closed ring enhancement with central necrosis, 7 mm midline shift, and markedly elevated rCBV are atypical for tumefactive MS, which typically shows open ring enhancement on the cortical side and low/normal rCBV

Central necrosis, thick irregular ring enhancement, and rCBV ratio 4.2 are hallmarks of WHO grade 4 biology; non-enhancing lower-grade gliomas do not produce necrotic ring-enhancing masses of this character

useless_tools.rationale: No seizure history or ongoing seizure activity; EEG does not diagnose brain tumors and adds cost without informing the diagnosis or management in this case
No cardiac indication; echocardiogram has no role in the diagnostic workup of suspected high-grade glioma absent a specific question such as suspected paraneoplastic endocarditis
No arrhythmia or palpitation history; cardiac monitoring is unrelated to the workup of a brain mass and adds cost without informing management
No acute cardiac indication; ECG is not part of the glioma diagnostic workup in the absence of a specific pre-operative cardiac concern

harmful_tools.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated with a large intracranial mass causing 7 mm of midline shift; the pressure gradient created by LP risks transtentorial herniation. Even when LP is otherwise safe, CSF analysis is low-yield for primary brain tumor diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede lumbar puncture in any suspected mass lesion to identify mass effect and herniation risk; LP is then recognised as contraindicated
Adequate pre-operative MRI characterization of the mass, edema, and proximity to eloquent cortex is standard of care before neurosurgical tissue acquisition

critical_actions: Obtain MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol) before any invasive procedure
Initiate dexamethasone (10 mg IV loading dose, then 4 mg IV every 6 hours) to reduce symptomatic vasogenic edema and mass effect
Obtain urgent neurosurgical consultation for tissue diagnosis (stereotactic biopsy or maximal safe resection) and operative planning
Obtain neuro-oncology consultation for multidisciplinary treatment planning and adjuvant therapy
Obtain pre-operative labs (CBC, BMP, coagulation, type and screen) before craniotomy or biopsy
Monitor blood glucose closely given corticosteroid use in a patient with type 2 diabetes; adjust antihyperglycemic therapy as needed
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform lumbar puncture given 7 mm midline shift — herniation risk
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide) before tissue diagnosis and molecular profiling are complete
Do not delay tissue diagnosis based on a presumptive ischemic TIA diagnosis — a non-resolving focal deficit with an enhancing necrotic mass on MRI mandates tumor workup
key_reasoning_points: A new progressive focal neurological deficit (right arm weakness, right inferior quadrantanopia) that does not resolve and is accompanied by morning-predominant headache in a man over 50 requires urgent contrast-enhanced MRI — it is not safe to attribute this to TIA without imaging

MRI demonstrating a large heterogeneously enhancing necrotic left posterior parietal mass with restricted diffusion at the enhancing rim, extensive vasogenic edema, and 7 mm midline shift is characteristic of a high-grade neoplasm, not an ischemic infarct

Perfusion MRI (markedly elevated rCBV ratio 4.2) and MR spectroscopy (Cho/NAA ratio 13.7, prominent lipid-lactate peaks) corroborate high-grade biology and guide biopsy targeting to the highest-grade region

Definitive WHO 2021 classification requires tissue with molecular profiling (IDH1/2, MGMT promoter methylation, TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification, 1p/19q codeletion); imaging cannot assign molecular subtype or grade
Mass effect with 7 mm midline shift renders lumbar puncture contraindicated; LP should not be performed to evaluate a suspected brain mass

The red herring of a provisional TIA diagnosis — plausible given the cardiovascular risk profile — must be resolved by imaging, which shows no ischemic infarct in an arterial distribution and instead reveals a necrotic enhancing mass

red_herrings.data_point: Provisional TIA diagnosis made at outside urgent care in the context of hypertension, diabetes, prior smoking, and subacute right-sided focal deficit
red_herrings.intended_effect: An agent anchored on the cardiovascular risk profile and step-wise symptom progression may pursue a vascular workup (carotid duplex, cardiac monitoring, echocardiogram) and delay or omit contrast MRI and neurosurgical referral
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Non-resolving focal deficits over days-to-weeks in an adult, especially with morning-predominant headache, are not consistent with TIA (which resolves within 24 hours); contrast MRI demonstrating a necrotic enhancing mass with surrounding edema and midline shift establishes a structural neoplastic cause and mandates tumor workup

metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required tools (MRI, labs, literature, neurosurgery consult, neuro-oncology consult), single diagnostic chain, classic ring-enhancing necrotic right parietal mass with high rCBV — unambiguous high-grade imaging pattern; one embedded red herring (provisional TIA) that resolves immediately on MRI
